title: Three questions one derivative answers
intro: Rates, direction, and the extreme that lives where the derivative isn't looking.

steps.title: Differentiate the relation, not the quantity
steps.body:
Related rates link two changing things through the geometry that connects them. A sphere inflating at constant volume rate Q: differentiate `V = (4/3)πr³` once to get `dV/dt = 4πr²·(dr/dt)`, so `dr/dt = Q/(4πr²)`.

Read the consequence: with Q constant, **dr/dt falls as the sphere grows**. Volume climbs linearly, radius only as t^(1/3) — the same inflow spread over an ever-larger surface. Tank pressurisation, `I = C·dV/dt`, `V = L·di/dt`: one geometric relation, differentiated once.

steps.title: Direction is the sign of f′
steps.body:
For `f(x) = x³ - 3x² - 9x + 15`, `f′(x) = 3(x - 3)(x + 1)` — increasing on (-∞, -1), decreasing on (-1, 3), increasing again on (3, ∞). The roots of f′ are the turning points.

A zero of f′ is **not** automatically an extremum. If f′ doesn't change sign across it, the curve pauses and carries on the same way: an inflection, not a peak.

points.label: f′ > 0
points.note: Increasing. Still climbing; a loss that is not yet falling.

points.label: f′ = 0
points.note: A turning point OR an inflection. The sign CHANGE decides which — the zero alone doesn't.

points.label: f′ < 0
points.note: Decreasing. Monotone discharge; a loss genuinely coming down.

steps.title: Classifying what you found
steps.body:
With f′(c) = 0: `f″(c) < 0` is a local **maximum**, `f″(c) > 0` a local **minimum**, and `f″(c) = 0` is **inconclusive** — fall back to the first-derivative test and read the sign change.

The worked classic: cut x × x corners from an S × S sheet and fold, giving `V(x) = x(S - 2x)²`. The maximum sits at **x = S/6**, which for S = 30 cm is 5 cm and 2000 cm³. The answer being a ratio is what makes it worth knowing — it transfers to any sheet.

steps.title: The extreme at the edge
steps.body:
On a closed interval, the absolute extreme can sit at an **endpoint**, where f′ says nothing. That same cubic on [-2, 6]:

| Point | f |
|---|---|
| x = -2 | 13 |
| x = -1 (local max) | 20 |
| x = 3 (local min) | -12 |
| x = 6 (endpoint) | **69** |

The interior peak is 20. The actual maximum is **69**, at the right endpoint, where f′(6) = 27 — nowhere near zero. An optimiser that only collects stationary points reports 20 and is wrong by a factor of three.

recap: Differentiate the relation to link rates. Read direction off the sign of f′ and confirm a turning point by the sign change, not the zero. Classify with f″, falling back when it vanishes. And on a closed interval, evaluate the endpoints — the derivative is blind to them, which is exactly why they get missed.
